explainer.title: Explain an alert (Ana: HR, HRV, sleep, CO2)
explainer.detector: Detector: anomaly 0.91. Main signals: heart rate, HRV, CO2.

passages.name: NASA-STD-3001 CO2 Technical Brief
passages.text:
Current NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 [V2 6004] limits the average 1-hour CO2 partial pressure (ppCO2) in the habitable volume to no more than 3 mmHg. Previous requirements accepted a larger range (3.8 to 7.5 mmHg) that has been lowered to 3 mmHg due to evidence from observed operational and research data.
Anecdotal evidence from previous spaceflight missions have found the following associations between CO2 levels and symptomology:
- Headaches at levels between 2.8-4.5 mmHg; worsening with increasing levels of CO2 accompanied by fatigue and malaise flushing.
- Fatigue malaise, decreased sleep, and nausea reported at levels above 4.5 mmHg.
If the average ppCO2 is exceeded over several days for unknown reasons, the Flight Control Team will take corrective actions to either identify, diagnose, and repair degraded CO2 scrubbing equipment or activate supplemental CO2 scrubbing equipment as needed.

explainer.title: Routine why: exercise and bone

passages.name: HRP Risk of Bone Fracture
passages.text:
Given the skeletal changes that occur during spaceflight, there is a possibility that the bones of crewmembers during and after spaceflight are not as strong as they were before spaceflight and a fracture may occur postflight for activities otherwise unlikely to induce fracture prior to space flight.
Extensive pre/post flight aBMD measurements exist for International Space Station (ISS) astronauts; exercise regimens using ARED/T2 (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device/Treadmill 2) six days/week have minimized deficits in postflight aBMDs.

passages.name: NASA-STD-3001 CO2 Technical Brief
passages.text:
Research and past historical data has revealed an association between reported headaches and CO2 levels among crewmembers.
- To keep the risk of headache below 1%, average 7-day CO2 needs to be maintained below 2.5 mmHg (current ISS range: 1 to 9 mmHg; 3001 standard requires <3 mmHg).
- Most experienced headaches were moderate intensity, requiring the use of analgesics in many cases.
Some observations suggest that what appears to be increased CO2 sensitivity during spaceflight may actually be attributed to individual predisposition to CO2 retention, adaption to microgravity, and local fluctuations of CO2 that are not measured by fixed sensors (Law, Watkins, & Alexander, 2010). Fluid shift due to decreased venous and lymphatic drainage in microgravity largely contributes to symptoms similar to CO2 over-exposure, including headaches.

explainer.title: Sleep debt: 'I've adapted'

passages.name: HRP Risk from Sleep Loss
passages.text:
Given that astronauts experience sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload, there is a possibility that performance decrements and adverse health outcomes will occur.
There is evidence of sleep deficiency inflight as crews sleep 6 h/night and increase their sleep and circadian misalignment. There is also evidence of work overload and scheduling issues. Ground studies demonstrate that despite perception that one can adapt, these risk factors cause short-term performance, mood, psychosocial, and metabolic decrements and are associated with long term poor health outcomes including increased risk of Alzheimer's Disease, cardiovascular disease, hormone-dependent cancer, and diabetes.

readings.text: elbow pain after EVA, on 100% oxygen now
readings.label: reported

passages.name: NASA-STD-3001 Habitable Atmosphere Technical Brief
passages.text:
Decompression sickness is caused by the evolution of dissolved nitrogen into gaseous state, forming bubbles as pressure decreases.
Types of Decompression Sickness
- Type 1: joint pain, single extremity tingling or numbness, and mild skin symptoms.
- Type 2: central nervous system or cardiovascular symptoms. Symptoms can range from muscle weakness, confusion, impaired balance, and stroke. Injuries can be fatal.
If DCS occurs, current treatment options include recompression to sea level pressure or higher (hyperbaric therapy), breathing 100% O2, and supportive care of any injuries or sequelae.
When DCS symptoms occur in space, returning to normal cabin environments may be enough to resolve symptoms. Alternatively, use of the cabin or even an EVA suit to raise ambient pressure to hyperbaric conditions may be considered.

explainer.title: Dose inside the shelter, passage doesn't say

readings.text: ALERT: solar particle event in progress. All crew in the storm shelter
readings.label: measured

passages.name: NASA-STD-3001 Radiation Protection Technical Brief
passages.text:
Solar Particle Events (SPE) – low to medium energy protons. Shielding (5-20 g/cm2 aluminum and polyethylene) IS effective. Countermeasures: Shielding, monitoring, accurate event determination, dosimetry, and timely reporting to alert crew to seek shelter are essential for crew safety.
Storm shelter: Additional Storm Shelter with an added 10 cm water equivalent in crew quarters to protect against centennial solar particle event. This can be achieved by rearranging items such as water containers and/or high hydrogen content materials. Timelines of SPEs allow sufficient time for re-configuration.
Radiation alerting provides an additional layer of protection to limit exposure to SPEs (early warning allows for crew to safe vehicle and configure shelter).
